strengths: SciEvents is a substantial and relevant resource: 2,508 abstracts, 24,381 events, and 56,411 arguments, with explicit coverage of discontinuous, overlapping, and hierarchical structures. Its contribution to scientific information extraction could remain valuable independently of the proposed model.

Dataset construction includes expert schema development, annotator training, separate quality inspection, and revision procedures. The extensive schema descriptions and annotated example make the task understandable.

The experiments cover nine baselines across several modeling families, report three independent runs and full precision/recall results, and include complex-structure analyses and ablations. The reported discontinuous-argument results are promising.
Equations, decoding pseudocode, hyperparameters, computational costs, annotation procedures, and a public repository link provide a useful foundation for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation comparability is unresolved. Appendix C says discriminative models are evaluated only on contiguous nuggets and generative models use offset-free evaluation, while Appendix B specifies exact token-span matching. It is unclear whether Table 3 uses identical gold instances and matching rules across systems, including repeated text mentions. This needs reconciliation through a common scorer and explicit treatment of unsupported structures before the state-of-the-art claim is established.

The grid representation loses information for valid event configurations. Algorithm 1 stores argument roles on nuggets and uses untyped trigger-to-argument head links. If a shared nugget is Subject of one FAC event and Object of another, decoding attaches both roles to both events, even with perfect grid predictions. Overlapping nuggets sharing a head introduce related ambiguities. The paper should report recovery from gold grids, quantify collisions, and resolve or explicitly delimit this representational limitation.

Annotation reliability is insufficiently quantified for a central dataset contribution. The 73.05% first-pass inspection acceptance rate measures a workflow outcome, not independent annotation agreement or residual error. A separately double-annotated sample with agreement on spans, types, roles, and hierarchical links would strengthen confidence. Operational guidelines for reverse-order nuggets and coreference also need clearer documentation.

The evidence for the model's specific contribution is limited. Overall gains over Tagprime are only 0.51 AC and 0.53 EC F1 points, without paired uncertainty analysis. Closely related word-word relation approaches, including W2NER-style modeling and the cited USM/Mirror frameworks, need stronger positioning and suitable comparisons. Moreover, removing the grid refiner improves discontinuous AC from 13.86 to 14.98 and reverse-order AC from 7.27 to 11.99, weakening the claimed consistency of its benefits.

The cross-domain conclusions exceed what Table 2 establishes. Density and complexity depend on annotation scope, schema, and document genre, so these comparisons cannot isolate intrinsic properties of scientific language. GENIA already supports nested events, yet its sub-event statistics are omitted and the discussion implies other datasets mainly capture overlap. The acknowledged restriction to ACL abstracts should also constrain the broader scientific-domain claims.

The complexity and decoding documentation need reconciliation. Appendix D describes overall quadratic complexity, while Appendix A acknowledges potentially exponential path enumeration. Skipping early validation does not bound inference-time decoding. Explicit traversal safeguards and validation settings are needed to reproduce this behavior. Together with the evaluation and representation concerns, these issues warrant revision before a positive Findings recommendation.
